articles.title: Season of protests
articles.content: A WAVE of protests is sweeping across the world in a season of unrest. From West to East, the street is confronting the state. Led predominantly by students and young people, protests have been widening to encompass other disaffected groups in society. In some cases, they are morphing into a nationwide movement. On almost every continent, governments are being put on notice that there will be a price to pay for misgovernance and being indifferent to public demands. India’sGen Z has been in the streetsin anti-government protests against the controversial revision of electoral rolls. Students in France beganprotestingagainst deteriorating school conditions with other groups, including trade unions, joining demonstrations over high living costs and inequality. In Italy, students, farmers and truckers took to the streets in protests driven by education costs, economic grievances, and anti-war sentiment. In Brussels, students marched over education funding. Spain saw protests over a housing crisis. In Albania, student-led demonstrations occurred over living costs and a controversial tourism project linked to Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law. In Portugal, protests erupted over housing and falling living standards. There were education protests across Greece. In Brazil, thousands joined a student march against the election bid of far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro. Tunisia’s capital witnessed protests demanding the president’s resignation and democratic rights. The triggers vary, as do the underlying causes. Each protest is rooted in its own political context. But there are common themes. All reject the status quo and indicate disenchantment with traditional political parties. All voice anger against unresponsive governments and the state failing them on their socioeconomic demands. The context for most protests is a cost-of-living crisis and deterioration or cuts in public services compounded by the state’s inability to deliver on education and jobs. Economic grievances and resentment of inequality are a driving force of the protests. A sense of disenfranchisement is another common thread. The heavy-handed response by governments to the protests and draconian crackdowns further fuelled the unrest and sparked violent clashes in several places. But it energised demonstrators to keep returning to the street. Unfortunately, in France protests degenerated intolooting and rioting. Protests in Europe and India share a defining feature. They are propelled by a wave of student activism. At their core is youth frustration in a generation that sees broken promises and an uncertain future. It feels betrayed by the lack of educational and economic opportunities. Protesters have also been venting rage against political leaders who have ignored public needs and are seen as venal. Initiated by young people, protests have expanded into broader movements as other disaffected groups, with their own set of demands, joined the demonstrations. Social media has been a key mobilisation tool in all the protests. Governments have been put on notice that misrule and ignoring public needs will have consequences. None of the protests or movements have been party-led. Political parties have largely been sidelined, even as they tried to leverage the demonstrations; France’s left aligned itself with the protesters. In several European countries, protests are playing out in an environment of deep polarisation, which parties of both the left and right are trying to exploit. This is especially because elections are due next year in many countries including France, Spain, and Italy. In India, the youth ‘Cockroach’ movement has spearheaded the protests and mounted the most significant challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government so far. The ongoing protests came against the backdrop of student protests led by the Cockroach party over the leak of exam papers in May, which forced the resignation of the education minister. This time, the catalyst was the revision of voter lists by India’s election commission, which apparently involved the removal of around 130 million voters. The government and the election commission’s claim that this was aimed at eliminating duplicate and ineligible entries was widely rejected. It was instead seen as a step towards mass disenfranchisement. It became thetrigger for youth protests, demanding the resignation of the chief election commissioner and scrapping the revision. India’s opposition parties also joined the demonstrations and decried the move as a politically motivated purge to benefit the ruling BJP. The Cockroach Janta Party used the opportunity to broaden its campaign. The government’s strong-arm tactics to suppress the popular upsurge only inflamed the demonstrators who accused Modi of “stealing democracy”. While these protests did not pose an existential threat to Modi, his jittery and increasingly autocratic government behaved as if they did — with arrests and a harsh clampdown. The scale of the protests and the government’s repressive response eroded Modi’s authority, weakened his grip on power, and dented his credibility and image. The mass protests signified much more than opposition to the voter roll overhaul. They have been about democratic rights and democratic accountability and against pervasive injustice. As Indian academic Sudhir Kumar Suthar has argued, they have been driven by the quest for dignity as much as for rights. The message from the young is clear: “they deserve a more dignified life than what they have received from the system so far.” The central question is what will be the outcome of mass protests and what will they achieve? A definitive assessment has to wait until the protests play themselves out as most are still unfolding. But one unintended consequence of the current wave of discontent in some European countries, especially France but to a degree also in Spain and Portugal, may be to strengthen the far-right. The far-right has led none of these protests but it stands to benefit from their fallout. In a political landscape where the political centre is being hollowed out and centrist parties have lost touch with young people, unrest advantages the most organised opposition force that promises order. In France, that force is Marine Le Pen’s Rassemblement National. Where the hard-right is in power the advantage works differently. It enables governments to cast the protests as a law-and-order issue fuelled by migrants to justify harsher measures. More generally, youth-led protests may force governments to take more seriously the needs and aspirations of young people which have rarely been a priority. What the streets are signalling is a breakdown of trust that can no longer be brushed aside. For now, the protests have put governments on notice: misrule has consequences. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.
articles.author: Maleeha Lodhi

articles.title: Pakistan’s global role
articles.content: THE nature of Pakistan’s role in global politics is once again the subject of much debate. Several officials areferrying messagesbetween Iran and the US for an end to the conflict, having helped organise a short-lived peace agreement earlier in the year. Based on these and past events, there are a series of judgement calls that observers make about the Pakistani state and its position in the world order. One set of views sees Pakistan as a client state of the US, that is, one that’s subservient to America’s imperial interests and its immediate allies in the region, the Gulf monarchies. This view is shared by sections of the left — globally, in the region, and within Pakistan — and disgruntled opponents of the current regime, who furnish as evidence for it the country’s role in global anti-communist politics in the 1950s and 1960s, its partnership with the US against the Soviets in Afghanistan, its role during the ‘war on terror’ between 2001 and 2013, and the proximity of ties with the Trump administration in recent months. Ironically, conservatives and Islamists also cite the 1950s/1960s and the experience of US-Pakistan relations during the war on terror and especially in the last few years, as evidence of successive regimes siding with global secularist interests in subjugating both Islamic movements in the region and Muslim political identity at home. The other view, held in the same time-space continuum, sees the country as ideologically fundamentalist, and simultaneously, a client of China and an unpredictable ally of the US — one that is capable of undermining the global hegemon on its own or in collaboration with the Chinese. This view is shared by much of the American and Indian mainstream, who cite CPEC and close military relations as an example of Chinese clientelism, previous support to the Taliban during the invasion of Afghanistan as an example of duplicity, and its approach to Kashmir, its recent diplomatic support for Iran, and the broader sociocultural and ideational life of its citizens, as an example of (religious) fundamentalism. As with most sweeping observations, many may detect a kernel of truth in these otherwise clearly contradictory positions. Close proximity to American imperial interests has characterised many passages in Pakistani political history. Similarly, the relationship with China remains remarkably consistent since the 1970s. However, in an effort to account for Pakistan’s global and regional behaviour, these observations lapse back to the rather broad and imprecise categories of ‘client state’ or ‘fundamentalist state’. The reality, just on the basis of the actions listed above, is that the state’s geopolitical and ideational positioning has varied considerably, which makes it hard to pin it down as a US ‘client’ of the same ilk as Japan/ South Korea or the Gulf monarchies, or as a Chinese client like North Korea. There are a series of judgement calls that observers make about the state’s position in the world order. What is consistent though is the subordinate role that the state here plays in global affairs, not just in terms of geopolitics but also — and more fundamentally — in terms of international economic processes. How does ‘subordinate’ differ from ‘client’? Beyond mere semantics, a substantive difference is that a subordinate actor may have limited agency, but it retains the capability of understanding and developing its own interests. A client, on the other hand, would, by and large replicate the interests of its patrons. On the evidence of the last seven decades, it would be incorrect to assert that the Pakistani state elite has not developed a sense of its own interests, even though some may disagree with the content of those interests or how those interests were developed. There is, for example, a long-standing recognition of being in a ‘tough’ geography, with insecure borders on at least three sides. There is also a persisting notion that it faces a periodically existential threat from a much more powerful eastern neighbour and that this threat should be countered by a military deterrent. This in turn can only be obtained by forging reciprocal relations with more powerful states. The presence of these interests/ ideas does not invalidate the fact that the state’s own actions and responses may have hastened insecurities in various ways. Nor can it paper over the fact that the processes through which the state recognises its context and develops its response are heavily skewed towards a largely insulated military-bureaucratic state apparatus. Both, in turn, lead to other domestic problems, including frequent civil-military political conflict and law and order insecurity in the peripheries. However, while some reduce Pakistan’s subordination to its geography or the original conditions of its creation, one can make the more substantive case that it remains in that place by the nature of the global economic order since the 1970s and due to its own economic dysfunction. With basic processes of capital accumulation stagnating or being rendered highly inefficient, the dollar requirement to ensure subsistence-level growth under global conditions of economic liberalisation can only be met through wilful subordination to varied benefactors. Periodic balance-of-payment crises since the 1980s have precipitated this pattern, and geopolitical posturing to extract IMF concessions or rents in other forms has cemented it. Each successive crisis of the last four decades has found resolution via subordination in the geopolitical domain: favour garnered with the Gulf monarchies via military assistance or labour provision in exchange for reserve deposits; providing the US with regional geopolitical support in exchange for IMF approval, or allowing Chinese capital to make infrastructure investments to kickstart (fleeting) economic growth. Ultimately, each temporary staving off of an economic crisis has pinned down the state’s subordinate position. And in the process little has been done to fix the underlying issue of domestic economic dysfunction. The writer teaches politics and sociology.
articles.author: Umair Javed

articles.title: The academic bubble
articles.content: In order to speak about the future one must first recognise the contemporary moment, as it is the contemporary moment that indicates the future — Alexandre Kojève UNIVERSITIES as places of higher learning have much to say about the future. They talk about AI advancements, new technologies and future skills. Neoliberal universities, however, rarely address the deep-rooted crises of contemporary times. There seems to be a significant disconnect between the everyday realities within a university and those outside it. This is especially troubling in disruptive times like the ones we live in. I write as a peace scholar who is simultaneously witnessing a critical moment in history and routine academic life inside universities. Global higher education is experiencing deep structural and financial strain. Universities in the UK for example, are facing serious financial turmoil, yet our local universities continue to import their failing neoliberal agendas. Academic institutions in both places seem to have lost touch with the current unsettling realities. Many scholars of international relations and peace studies view the current moment as a paradigm-shifting moment in history. We see collapse and chaos all around with brutal genocides in Gaza, Sudan, and Congo, senseless wars in Iran, West Asia, and Ukraine, and illegal interventions in Venezuela and Cuba. Some view the current events as an end to the America-led order, while others view them as the collapse of the post-World War II international rules-based order and the rise of a multipolar or a pluriversal order. Some observers, such as Owen Jones, see a bigger collapse of Western dominance. Some describe the present turmoil as the end of capitalism itself. What is happening in our universities as the world falls apart? An ecological collapse is another reality of the present times. The UN has warned of “a point of no return” as we cross the 1.5 degrees Celsius limit in the next few years. The death toll from climate disasters continues to rise, with the devastation caused by the glacier collapse in Nepal, the agonising heatwaves in Europe, and the forest fires in Indonesia, Algeria, Canada, and Europe. But all this does not stop capitalist greed, which continues to create a global climate emergency. So what is happening in our universities as the world falls apart? Lost in the ranking race, they appear inundated with papers, conferences, and funded projects as publication numbers skyrocket, citation scores pile up, and academics are told they cannot pause or they will perish. Hence, the meaning and purpose of knowledge seem to be lost in neoliberal academia. AI adds further layers to the meaningless reproduction of knowledge. Despite an intensifying climate emergency, big tech companies continue to sell visions of AI futures, and universities continue to impose narratives about AI inevitability as if its massive environmental footprint is a secondary issue. We are facing urgent questions about the role of academia in supporting harmful extractive logics that lead to an ecological collapse. There are also serious questions about universities’ complicity in ongoing genocides as evident in the case of student protests for Gaza, which were brutally suppressed by big universities. However, instead of addressing such pressing questions, universities continue to reinforce “the very logic that produced the crises”. Urgent and fundamental transformation in our way of thinking is needed. Educational spaces offer hope. They must indulge in greater deliberation to reimagine the future. Decolonial imagination has recently gained traction across global academia and social movements. Decolonial thinking questions modern paradigms of rationality that view knowledge as private property and research as data extraction. Instead, it explores indigenous knowledge systems based on relationality. Indigenous cultures have survived on this planet for thousands of years without sophisticated theories of survival and security. They have lived respectfully with the Earth without any technical knowledge of sustainability. The present moment demands that universities pause. They must also halt the ranking race and think about deeper, fundamental questions, such as what is the purpose of knowledge creation? Individual success cannot be the purpose of knowledge creation in times of collective failure. The academic fixation with publication metrics is a distraction from the real purpose of knowledge creation, which lies in addressing the grave crises of our times. If universities wish to remain relevant in the future, they must redirect their energies towards building livable futures for all. The writer is director, Centre for Critical Peace Studies at the University of Management & Technology & founder of The Pluriversity Lahore.
articles.author: Fatima Waqi Sajjad

articles.title: AI agenda
articles.content: WHEN asked what he would dress up as for Halloween, a 10-year-old boy I know responded, “Claude, because there’s nothing scarier than AI.” Whether you consider this funny or astute, it highlights the pervasiveness of the AI bogeyman. And the best thing to do with your fears is face them. So it was good to see Pakistan play a prominent role at the recent Global Digital and AI Summit in Seoul and ramp up engagement with the World Bank to support the country’s digital transformation through a Digital and AI Compact. Pakistan has committed to spending $1 billion on AI by 2030 and is cracking on with plans to digitise 12 key sectors by 2035 under the National Digital Master Plan. As the momentum builds, we must ask: how will Pakistan fund investment in AI? And what makes digital transformation and AI adoption capable of overcoming structural issues that have held back traditional activities like manufacturing? AI use — particularly localised AI development and large language model (LLM) training — requires an immense and stable energy supply, high-speed internet and data storage, none of which are readily available in Pakistan. While efforts are underway to boost 5G spectrum and satellite access, the electricity sector is plagued by outages, a dilapidated grid, and circular debt. Concerns abound about whether Pakistan’s scarce water supply can bear the burden of water-guzzling data centres. Then there’s the question of how to insulate the future of Pakistani youth from widespread AI adoption. Pakistan’s first economic census last year identified that the services sector makes up over 50 per cent of the country’s economy (production is less than 30pc). How will Pakistan fund investment into AI? A recent World Bank report notes that the services sector is most vulnerable to AI adoption, with 61pc of Pakistani service workers in jobs with higher-than-average AI exposure. Based on 2024 data, the report indicates that 8pc of all jobs are at risk of being replaced by AI (a number likely to rise). This means many Pakistanis will be trapped in low-skill, low-paying, and climate-vulnerable agricultural or manual labour jobs, while a sliver of society benefits from productivity gains. The other question is how to prevent the complete securitisation of the AI agenda, a common challenge in countries with national security preoccupations. Concerns about the use of LLMs for mass surveillance have been voiced in the US and China, a scenario that Pakistan, with its punitive electronic crime legislation, is well primed for. Early interest has also been expressed in using AI for smart policing and biometric identity management. An early, advanced data centre was built under a National Aerospace Science and Technology Park initiative. The state will feel a growing need to direct AI investment towards national security, because it’s only a matter of time before local terrorist groups begin deploying AI in anti-state activities. Writing in South Asian Voices, Zohaib Altaf and Nimrah Javed highlight the risk of such groups using AI to better target attacks based on intelligence analysis or to support arms development, particularly weaponised drones. The precedent for this has already been set by the Houthis in Yemen, so the likelihood of AI investment being funnelled primarily to military ends is high. If Pakistan’s AI agenda is not carefully monitored, we face a future in which limited digital infrastructure in the form of resource-intensive data centres is reserved for security-linked AI use, with some private enterprises enjoying gains at the expense of the wider population. In this scenario, urban youth unemployment increases and rural poverty intensifies; agricultural employment survives the AI rollout, but is ravaged by climate change instead. There is a way to prevent this scenario. That’s through high levels of transparency and accountability in AI governance, regulation, and investment, including the requirement for public service considerations and consultation as part of all investments. Pakistan’s civil society organisations and media should also redouble efforts to understand the implications of AI investment to ensure accountability. On a more positive note, the notions of accountability and transparency in AI are no longer antithetical to AI development. US-based civic activism against data centres on resource-use grounds is increasingly effective in blocking projects. And while Big Tech has thrown up its hands, arguing that it can’t be held responsible for what LLMs do, new research suggests that LLMs may be easier to unpick (and so monitor) than we think. Such public-interest considerations, particularly with an inclusion lens, should be part of Pakistan’s AI journey. That may make it less scary. The writer is a political and integrity risk analyst.
articles.author: Huma Yusuf

articles.title: Wheat price dilemma
articles.content: THE announcement of anindicative wheat priceof Rs4,500 per 40 kilograms may have come too late for Sindh farmers, but it is welcome as far as it goes. That is not far. The figure is Rs1,000 higher than last year’s and, by the government’s account, reflects rising production and fuel costs. It is also Rs500 short of what farmers demanded. And there is no word on who will buy the grain or when. An indicative price is a signal, not a guarantee. Since April 2025, when the government dropped the support price and suspended large-scale procurement, farmers have been promised a market-based system that would serve them better. It has not. The crop now being sown is the third to go into the ground without a floor.Punjab’s experiencethis April shows what happens when a procurement price is announced without a mechanism to enforce it. The province tried to revive buying through bank-backed private aggregators. The banks doubted the scheme’s viability, and the aggregators bought only 160,000 tonnes against a target of 2.5m tonnes. Prices fell anyway. A price no buyer is obliged or financially equipped to pay is only a number. Growers seem to have grasped this before the government did. Consumers, meanwhile, are not being spared. Over five years the price of wheat has gone up by 150pc, and that rise goes straight to the price of flour. Punjab has used the price as its only tool instead of working on the cost of farm inputs, which the federal government’s policies have kept high. Flour in cities is selling for Rs160-190 per kilogram, which is hard on poor households. Even the government’s stocks are expensive. Sindh began selling government wheat this month at Rs12,500 per 100kg, or Rs5,000 per 40kg. That is more than the prime minister has offered farmers. The test of wheat reform is not whether the government can step out of the market. It is whether the system that replaces government buying shares the risk fairly among farmers, traders, millers, banks, and the state, keeps flour affordable, and protects the country’s food supply. For now, farmers carry most of the risk while everyone else looks after their own interests. With sowing already underway, the government should say in plain terms what it will buy, through which agency, with what money, and by when. It should adapt its imports to that plan. It should look at the cost of fertiliser and other inputs, instead of relying on price alone. And it should help poor households directly, instead of keeping flour cheap for all by squeezing the grower. A price announcement with no buyer behind it will not persuade anyone to sow, and a market that works for only one side is not worth defending.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Encounter culture
articles.content: Ten suspected criminals killed in Karachi police ‘encounters’ in two days should trouble anyone concerned about public safety and the rule of law. Sevendiedin separate incidents on Thursday and another three on Friday. In each case, police reported armed resistance, exchanges of fire, and the recovery of weapons.These accounts may be accurate, but cannot be accepted without scrutiny. Officers confronting armed criminals have every right to defend themselves and others. Karachi’s residents, long exposed to street crime and violent robberies, deserve protection. Yet the frequency of these so-called encounters raises questions about how operations are conducted and whether suspects are given an opportunity to surrender. Whether the police actions were legitimate or unlawful can only be established through credible investigations. There must be forensic examination of weapons, independent verification of police accounts, and proper documentation of injuries and evidence. Such scrutiny should be routine whenever police gunfire causes death, regardless of the victim’s alleged criminal history. Otherwise, the public must rely entirely on the version offered by those who pulled the trigger. The concern extends beyond Karachi. In Punjab, where the Crime Control Department faces allegations of staged encounters, the political response has exposed a dangerous willingness to equate police killings with justice. After a suspect in the killing of a teenage worker in Multan died in analleged encounter, PML-N lawmaker Hina Parvez Butt celebrated it as “justice served immediately”. She deleted the post butdefendedher remarks as public sentiment. Anger over a child’s murder is understandable. But an elected representative ought to know that public outrage cannot substitute for a trial, and that a police killing is not a judicial verdict. Punjab Information Minister Azma Bokhari criticised the comments, though the issue is larger than one politician’s embarrassment. Governments must make clear that police performance will be judged by crimes prevented, offenders lawfully arrested, and cases successfully prosecuted, not bodies counted. Independent inquiries into disputed encounters should publish findings and establish responsibility if unlawful force is proved. Police officers need training, equipment and supervision that make arrest a realistic option where possible. A force that can shoot but cannot build a case offers little lasting security. The police are duty-bound to protect lives. They do not have a licence to kill.
articles.author: Editorial
